sections.html: Gainesville has 151,275 residents and is both the Alachua County seat and its biggest city. The University of Florida and Santa Fe College bring so many students that median age is 26.4, which means buyers tend to be a blend of owner-occupants and investors. The rest of this page covers what a seller needs to know about the tax bill.

sections.h2: Who bills a Gainesville tax bill
sections.html:
Billing comes from Alachua County, not the city. The county property appraiser handles value and exemptions, the tax collector handles mailing and collection, and the city is just one of the bodies whose rates appear on the bill.

  • Tax collector: phone (352) 374-5236 if no bill arrives in November. Delinquent-tax payment questions go to its Tax Operations Department at (352) 264-6968.
  • Property appraiser: prepares the tax roll and decides homestead, disability, widow and agricultural exemptions. Its tangible division answers at (352) 374-5234.
  • City commission: sets the city millage as part of its annual budget.
  • County commission: sets county millage and certain non-ad valorem assessments.

Non-ad valorem charges on a bill can include mandatory refuse collection, rural collection center, solid waste management, paving, water extension, fire, storm water and PACE assessments. Lower-income owners may be excused from some of them through the county social services office at (352) 264-6750.

If you have moved or sold recently, make sure the bill is going to the right person. Send the appraiser your new mailing address, and tell your buyer or closing agent which tax year's bill is still outstanding. A bill that lands in an old mailbox still carries the same due dates.

The city's rate for fiscal year 2027 is 6.7297 mills, meaning $6.7297 per $1,000 of taxable value. Its rolled-back rate is 6.3839, and the two-thirds vote maximum is 7.0223.

Those numbers cover the city alone. Your parcel also carries lines from the county, the school board and the water district, and the TRIM notice and September hearings can still shift the final figures. The November bill shows what was set, and the tax collector can confirm it.

sections.h2: Due dates and the early-payment discount
sections.html:
Expect your statement in the mailbox by the first of November. You can pay the full amount any time through March 31, and delinquency begins April 1. What you save for paying early shrinks every month.

Alachua County discount by month paid
Month paidDiscount
November4%
December3%
January2%
February1%
MarchNone

If a lender escrows for you, it asks for the bill itself and your copy is informational. It has to pay within the 4 percent window. Once a loan is paid off, the lender is supposed to remove your account from its list, so confirm that the bill now comes to you if you recently cleared a mortgage.

Accounts whose tax last year topped $100 can split this year's bill into four payments through the county tax collector. You must sign up by April 30.

  • June 30: first payment, with a 6 percent reduction.
  • September 30: second payment, 4.5 percent reduction.
  • December 31: third payment, 3 percent reduction.
  • March 31: final payment at full price.

Payments one and two are each a quarter of the previous year's tax. Payments three and four divide whatever is left of the real liability. If the June payment is skipped, you are out for the year and a regular November bill comes. When a due date lands on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Any real estate tax still open on April 1 draws a minimum 3 percent charge. During May each late parcel is advertised in a local paper for three weeks, and the cost is added to what you owe. The collector then holds an online certificate sale at lienhub.com on or before June 1.

Bidding starts at 18 percent and runs downward. The certificate pays its holder at least 5 percent unless the winning bid is zero, and it is a first lien that lasts seven years. Once two years run from the delinquency, the holder may request a tax deed, and the parcel then goes to public auction. You clear the lien by paying the collector.

Late taxes can be paid with cash, check, money order, debit card (minimum $2.50 fee), e-check ($1.00) or credit card and PayPal (2.5 percent fee). What you owe depends on the day the office receives the money.

If you run a business or rent out a home, the furniture, fixtures and equipment there are taxed as tangible personal property, and so are structural additions to mobile homes. The Alachua County Property Appraiser values these items each January 1, based on a return that the owner files. File between January 1 and April 1 and you earn an exemption of up to $25,000; a late or missing return brings penalties and forfeits it.

Unpaid personal property tax is late on April 1, when a $10 fee and 1.5 percent monthly interest begin. On May 1 the collector adds a collection fee of 20 percent of the gross tax, and a warrant adds a $50 legal fee. Call the tangible division at (352) 374-5234.

Homestead takes up to $50,000 off taxable value. File with the property appraiser by March 1, and remember the home must be your permanent residence. A statutory cap on assessed value growth, shown as 2.7 percent for 2026 on the state chart, protects owners, though a sale resets the next owner to just value.

The tax collector also offers a deferral. It is secured by a lien, carries interest capped at 7 percent a year, requires that the primary mortgage not exceed 70 percent of assessed value, and calls for proof of insurance. A change of ownership makes the whole deferred amount payable, so the closing agent must pay it.

Start by ordering a payoff from the Alachua County Tax Collector, and add any deferral balance to it. Your closing agent pays everything out of your proceeds. Tangible tax on a business or rental is prorated between buyer and seller at closing, and a lien for that tax survives a sale, so owners of rentals should confirm no personal property bill is open.

The tax year is January to December and the bill arrives in November. A spring closing may therefore still involve a bill you must settle. Cash buyers often agree to short timelines, which helps when April 1 delinquency is close.

Keep the paperwork in order. Pull your parcel record, confirm who receives the tax bill, request the payoff, and ask the title agent for a draft settlement statement before closing day. Check that each tax line matches the collector's number. If you rent the home, also gather the lease and any records of furniture or appliances left for tenants, since the appraiser may ask about them.

faqs.q: What is the Gainesville millage rate?
faqs.a: The city's rate for fiscal year 2027 is 6.7297 mills. County, school and water district lines are added on top, and the final rates appear on your November bill or from the Alachua County Tax Collector.
The Alachua County Tax Collector. If you do not get a November bill, call (352) 374-5236.

faqs.q: When is Alachua County property tax late?
faqs.a: After March 31. Taxes become delinquent April 1, and a 3 percent minimum charge is added.

faqs.q: When can I apply for the Gainesville installment plan?
faqs.a: Sign-up closes April 30 each year, and the first payment is due June 30. The accounts must have owed more than $100 the year before.

faqs.q: Does a sale end my homestead deferral?
faqs.a: The deferral becomes due, with interest, when ownership changes. The closing agent should pay the balance from your proceeds.
